::: {.objectives}
**Goals.** Compute net squared displacement and classify movement strategies
by fitting competing models; measure straightness across scales; find the
scale of area-restricted search with first-passage time; segment a track with
a threshold where that is honest; run behavioural change-point analysis and
test whether its answer survives a change of fix rate.

**Time:** ~75 minutes. **Packages:** `amt`, `adehabitatLT`, `bcpa`, `dplyr`,
`tidyr`, `lubridate`, `ggplot2`.
:::

```{r}
library(amt)
library(adehabitatLT)
library(bcpa)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(lubridate)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Setup — tracks from Sessions 1–3

```{r}
buffalo <- read.csv("data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz") |>
  transmute(id = individual.local.identifier,
            t  = as.POSIXct(timestamp, tz = "UTC"),
            x  = location.long, y = location.lat) |>
  filter(!is.na(x), !is.na(y)) |>
  distinct(id, t, .keep_all = TRUE)

trk <- make_track(buffalo, x, y, t, id = id, crs = 4326) |>
  transform_coords(crs_to = 32736)

vulture <- read.csv("data/vulture_leo.csv.gz") |>
  transmute(t = as.POSIXct(timestamp, tz = "UTC"),
            x = location.long, y = location.lat) |>
  filter(!is.na(x)) |>
  distinct(t, .keep_all = TRUE)

# Leo spans 47 degrees of latitude: no UTM zone fits, so use a global
# equal-area projection (EPSG:6933)
leo <- make_track(vulture, x, y, t, crs = 4326) |>
  transform_coords(crs_to = 6933)
```

## Task 1 — Net squared displacement

`adehabitatLT` computes NSD for you: it is the `R2n` column.

```{r}
cilla <- trk |> filter(id == "Cilla")
ltr <- as.ltraj(xy = as.data.frame(cilla[, c("x_", "y_")]),
                date = cilla$t_, id = "Cilla")
nsd_cilla <- ld(ltr) |> transmute(t = date, nsd_km2 = R2n / 1e6)

leo_ltr <- as.ltraj(xy = as.data.frame(leo[, c("x_", "y_")]),
                    date = leo$t_, id = "Leo")
nsd_leo <- ld(leo_ltr) |> transmute(t = date, nsd_km2 = R2n / 1e6)
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-align: center
bind_rows(mutate(nsd_cilla, who = "Buffalo 'Cilla'"),
          mutate(nsd_leo,   who = "Vulture 'Leo'")) |>
  ggplot(aes(t, nsd_km2)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#1f6f78", linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ who, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "NSD (km²)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Your turn

**1a.** Describe each curve in one sentence. Which looks resident, which migratory?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

Cilla's NSD rises quickly to a ceiling and fluctuates below it: once she has
explored her range she cannot get further from the start — a **resident**.

Leo's NSD shows six annual cycles: a rise (autumn migration), a plateau
(wintering), a fall (spring migration), a plateau (breeding) — the textbook
**migratory** profile. The next task makes that judgement quantitative.
:::

## Task 2 — Classify the strategy by fitting models

Bunnefeld et al. (2011): fit one model per strategy and compare. We fit on
**daily** mean positions to keep the curves manageable.

```{r}
daily_nsd <- function(tr) {
  d <- tr |>
    mutate(day = as_date(t_)) |>
    group_by(day) |>
    summarise(x = mean(x_), y = mean(y_), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(day)
  data.frame(t = as.numeric(d$day - d$day[1]),
             nsd = ((d$x - d$x[1])^2 + (d$y - d$y[1])^2) / 1e6)   # km²
}

fit_strategies <- function(d) {
  D <- max(d$nsd)
  ctl <- nls.control(maxiter = 500, warnOnly = TRUE)
  half_up   <- d$t[which.max(d$nsd > D / 2)]
  half_down <- d$t[nrow(d) - which.max(rev(d$nsd) > D / 2) + 1]
  fits <- list(
    nomad     = try(nls(nsd ~ b * t, d, start = list(b = D / max(d$t))), silent = TRUE),
    resident  = try(nls(nsd ~ c * (1 - exp(-k * t)), d,
                        start = list(c = median(d$nsd), k = 0.05), control = ctl), silent = TRUE),
    disperser = try(nls(nsd ~ dd / (1 + exp((th - t) / ph)), d,
                        start = list(dd = D, th = half_up, ph = 5), control = ctl), silent = TRUE),
    migrant   = try(nls(nsd ~ dd / (1 + exp((th1 - t) / ph1)) - dd / (1 + exp((th2 - t) / ph2)), d,
                        start = list(dd = D, th1 = half_up, ph1 = 5, th2 = half_down, ph2 = 5),
                        control = ctl), silent = TRUE)
  )
  fits[!vapply(fits, inherits, logical(1), "try-error")]
}

aic_table <- function(fits) {
  a <- vapply(fits, AIC, numeric(1))
  data.frame(model = names(a), dAIC = round(a - min(a))) |> arrange(dAIC)
}
```

Leo, June 2007 to June 2008:

```{r}
leo_07 <- leo |> filter(t_ >= as.POSIXct("2007-06-01", tz = "UTC"),
                        t_ <  as.POSIXct("2008-06-01", tz = "UTC"))
fits_leo <- suppressWarnings(fit_strategies(daily_nsd(leo_07)))
aic_table(fits_leo)
```

The migrant model wins by a mile. Now **read its parameters**:

```{r}
cf <- coef(fits_leo$migrant)
c(migration_distance_km = sqrt(cf[["dd"]]),
  departs_day = cf[["th1"]], returns_day = cf[["th2"]])

as.Date("2007-06-01") + round(c(cf[["th1"]], cf[["th2"]]))   # as calendar dates
```

### Your turn

**2a.** Fit the four models to every buffalo. What wins?
**2b.** For the "migrants", what is the migration distance? Are they migrants?
**2c.** Fit Leo's 2011–2012 year. What goes wrong, and why?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
strategy_summary <- function(tr, label) {
  f <- suppressWarnings(fit_strategies(daily_nsd(tr)))
  a <- aic_table(f)
  best <- a$model[1]
  dist <- if (best == "migrant" || best == "disperser") sqrt(abs(coef(f[[best]])[["dd"]])) else NA
  data.frame(animal = label, days = nrow(daily_nsd(tr)), best = best,
             runner_up_dAIC = a$dAIC[2], displacement_km = round(dist, 1))
}

bind_rows(lapply(unique(trk$id), \(i) strategy_summary(filter(trk, id == i), i)))
```

Three buffalo come out as **migrants** — with "migration" distances of 10 to
14 km. That is a shift to another part of the home range for a few weeks or
months, not a migration. The double-sigmoid is the most flexible of the four
curves, so it fits any excursion-and-return, and with hundreds of
autocorrelated daily points AIC differences are hugely inflated.

Look also at `runner_up_dAIC`: for several buffalo the second-best model is
within a few AIC units of the winner. The data barely separate the stories.

```{r}
leo_11 <- leo |> filter(t_ >= as.POSIXct("2011-06-01", tz = "UTC"),
                        t_ <  as.POSIXct("2012-06-01", tz = "UTC"))
strategy_summary(leo_11, "Leo 2011-12")
range(leo_11$t_)
```

Leo, a known migrant, is classified as a **disperser** in 2011–12. The reason
is in the dates: that year's data stop in the middle of the season, so only
the outbound half of the cycle is present — which *is* a single sigmoid step.
An incomplete cycle cannot show a return.

**The lesson:** model-based NSD classification is powerful, but only on
complete cycles, and only if you read the parameters. A classification
without a displacement distance and dates is not a result.
:::

## Task 3 — Straightness across scales

Straightness index = net displacement / path length, computed over a moving
window.

```{r}
hourly <- cilla |>
  track_resample(rate = hours(1), tolerance = minutes(10)) |>
  filter_min_n_burst(min_n = 3)

straightness <- function(tr, window_h) {
  tr |>
    mutate(win = floor(as.numeric(difftime(t_, min(t_), units = "hours")) / window_h)) |>
    group_by(burst_, win) |>
    filter(n() >= 0.8 * window_h) |>
    summarise(net  = sqrt((last(x_) - first(x_))^2 + (last(y_) - first(y_))^2),
              path = sum(sqrt(diff(x_)^2 + diff(y_)^2)), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(st = net / path)
}

st_tab <- lapply(c(3, 6, 12, 24, 72), function(w) {
  s <- straightness(hourly, w)
  data.frame(window_h = w, windows = nrow(s), median_ST = round(median(s$st), 3))
}) |> bind_rows()
st_tab
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What this shows

The same buffalo is "straight" over 3 hours and "tortuous" over 3 days:
straightness falls steadily as the window grows, because over longer periods
the path doubles back on itself. A straightness index is meaningless without
its window, and comparing indices computed over different windows is comparing
different things.

Straightness is at its best for **oriented** movement over a defined journey —
a homing bird, a migrating vulture between two stopovers — where the window is
set by the biology rather than by you.
:::

## Task 4 — First-passage time

```{r}
radii <- c(100, 250, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 3000, 4000, 5000, 6000)
f <- fpt(ltr, radii = radii, units = "hours")

vl <- varlogfpt(f, graph = FALSE)
fpt_profile <- data.frame(radius_m = radii, var_log_fpt = as.numeric(vl))
fpt_profile
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-align: center
ggplot(fpt_profile, aes(radius_m, var_log_fpt)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#1f6f78") + geom_point(colour = "#1f6f78", size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Radius (m)", y = "Variance of log(FPT)",
       title = "Cilla: first-passage time profile") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Your turn

**4a.** Where is the peak that indicates area-restricted search?
**4b.** Plot FPT at that radius along the track. When does Cilla linger?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

The variance is highest at the smallest radii — but there it measures resting
and GPS noise, not search. It falls to a minimum around 1.5 km and **peaks
again near 4 km**: the scale at which Cilla's use of space is most uneven,
i.e. the size of the patches she responds to.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-align: center
peak_r <- fpt_profile |> filter(radius_m >= 1000) |> slice_max(var_log_fpt) |> pull(radius_m)
peak_r

data.frame(t = ld(ltr)$date, fpt_h = f[[1]][, which(radii == peak_r)]) |>
  ggplot(aes(t, fpt_h)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#1f6f78", linewidth = 0.3) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = sprintf("FPT at %d m (hours)", peak_r)) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Long first-passage times mark periods when Cilla stayed within a few
kilometres for days; short ones mark relocations. Session 7 asks *why* —
which habitats hold her.
:::

## Task 5 — Thresholds: one honest, one not

```{r}
leo_daily <- leo |>
  mutate(day = as_date(t_)) |>
  group_by(day) |>
  summarise(x = mean(x_), y = mean(y_), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(day) |>
  mutate(km = c(NA, sqrt(diff(x)^2 + diff(y)^2)) / 1000)

cilla_hourly_speed <- hourly |> steps_by_burst() |>
  mutate(km_h = (sl_ / 1000) / as.numeric(dt_, units = "hours"))
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-align: center
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(log10(leo_daily$km + 1), breaks = 50, col = "#1f6f78", border = "white",
     main = "Leo: daily displacement", xlab = "log10(km + 1)")
hist(log10(cilla_hourly_speed$km_h + 0.001), breaks = 50, col = "#1f6f78",
     border = "white", main = "Cilla: hourly speed", xlab = "log10(km/h)")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

### Your turn

**5a.** Where would you put a threshold for each animal? Can you defend it?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

Leo's histogram has **two clearly separated modes** — resident days of a few
kilometres, migration days of a hundred or more — with an empty valley in
between. Any threshold in the valley gives the same answer, so a threshold is
transparent and honest:

```{r}
leo_daily |>
  filter(km > 50) |>
  count(month = month(day, label = TRUE), name = "migration_days")
```

Migration days fall in spring and autumn, exactly as the NSD model said.

Cilla's hourly speeds form one broad, skewed hump. There is no valley, so
wherever you put the line, you have made the answer rather than found it. That
is precisely the situation in which you need a model that assigns states
probabilistically and uses the fact that behaviour persists in time —
Session 8's hidden Markov models.
:::

## Task 6 — Behavioural change-point analysis

BCPA on persistence velocity $V\cos\theta$, for the first 25 days of Cilla's
hourly track.

```{r}
win <- cilla |> arrange(t_) |> filter(t_ < min(t_) + days(25))

run_bcpa <- function(d, windowsize) {
  vt <- GetVT(MakeTrack(d$x_, d$y_, d$t_))
  set.seed(1)
  ws <- WindowSweep(vt, "V*cos(Theta)", windowsize = windowsize,
                    progress = FALSE, K = 2)
  list(vt = vt, ws = ws, cps = ChangePointSummary(ws, clusterwidth = 3))
}

b1 <- run_bcpa(win, windowsize = 50)
nrow(b1$cps$phases)
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-align: center
plot(b1$vt$T.POSIX, b1$vt$V * cos(b1$vt$Theta), type = "l", col = "grey60",
     xlab = "", ylab = "V cos(θ)  (m/h)", main = "Cilla: BCPA change points")
abline(v = b1$cps$breaks$middle.POSIX, col = "firebrick", lty = 2)
```

### Your turn

**6a.** Rerun with `windowsize = 30`. **6b.** Resample to 3-hourly and rerun
with a window covering the same *time* (17 fixes ≈ 50 hours). **6c.** How many
change points survive both analyses?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
b1_30 <- run_bcpa(win, windowsize = 30)

win_3h <- win |> track_resample(rate = hours(3), tolerance = minutes(15))
b3_17  <- run_bcpa(win_3h, windowsize = 17)
b3_50  <- run_bcpa(win_3h, windowsize = 50)

data.frame(
  analysis = c("hourly, 50-fix window", "hourly, 30-fix window",
               "3-hourly, 17-fix window (~50 h)", "3-hourly, 50-fix window (~150 h)"),
  phases = c(nrow(b1$cps$phases), nrow(b1_30$cps$phases),
             nrow(b3_17$cps$phases), nrow(b3_50$cps$phases))
)
```

The count moves with every choice you make. The honest question is not "how
many phases?" but "which change points are **robust**?":

```{r}
cp_1h <- b1$cps$breaks$middle.POSIX
cp_3h <- b3_17$cps$breaks$middle.POSIX

matched <- vapply(cp_1h, \(tt) any(abs(difftime(cp_3h, tt, units = "hours")) <= 6),
                  logical(1))
c(hourly_change_points = length(cp_1h),
  also_found_at_3h_within_6h = sum(matched),
  share_robust = round(mean(matched), 2))
```

About three quarters of the hourly change points reappear within six hours
in the 3-hourly analysis. Those are the ones worth interpreting as changes in
the buffalo's behaviour. The remaining quarter appear only at one resolution:
treat them as properties of the window and the sampling until shown otherwise.
:::

## Self-check

::: {.quiz}
Turning angles of a track sampled every 6 hours are close to uniform. What
does this tell you?

- [ ] The animal moves at random
- [x] Directional persistence operates on a shorter timescale than 6 hours
- [ ] The resampling introduced an error
- [ ] GPS error dominates

::: {.quiz-feedback}
Persistence is a short-term property: over six hours the animal has changed
activity several times, so one step's direction says little about the next.
That is a statement about the **timescale of the behaviour relative to your
sampling**, not about the animal being random.
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
A disperser model fits a known migrant best. Most likely cause?

- [ ] The animal changed strategy
- [x] The data cover only part of the annual cycle
- [ ] AIC is unreliable for non-linear models
- [ ] The CRS is wrong

::: {.quiz-feedback}
A migration observed only on the way out *is* a single step up in NSD — the
disperser curve. Classify only complete cycles, and check the dates of your
data before interpreting any strategy.
:::
:::
